extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of hydrostatics / natural philosophers performing and interpreting fluid experiments (18th‑century experimental readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A collected set of experimental laws, paradoxes, and practical instructions for constructing and reasoning about fountains, tubes, and pressures in fluids; aimed at explaining and predicting fluid behaviour in experiments and devices. Emphasises how pressures depend on depth/geometry and how to compute net forces from stacked water and air columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Net driving force for outlet (fountain) by difference of acting forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The Difference of both these acting Powers ... the Difference is found by Substracting the smallest downward‑pressing Force a and e together ... from the greatest a, b and d together, less c ... So that the Difference, or the Force wherewith the Water ascends at M O, is equal to b and d, less e and less e, or to 162 Pounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked numerical example: compute upward and downward pressures contributed by named water and air columns, then subtract the smaller (downward) from the larger (upward) to get the net force driving the jet. The text demonstrates step‑by‑step symbolic bookkeeping (letters for columns) and a numeric instantiation producing 162 Pounds net upward force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fountain jet force formula (weight of water columns minus weight of air columns)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Water ... will be protruded out of the Cock M O with a Force equal to the Weight of both the Water‑Columns R and Y Z, Substracting the Gravity of the two Air‑Columns T 3 and 4 M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the weights of the water columns pushing up and subtract the weights of the interposed air columns pressing down. This gives a direct criterion to estimate the jet's driving force; the text notes one may neglect the air weight in many practical cases (see separate entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglectability of air weight in many hydrostatic calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Now since the Weight of the Air with Respect that of Water, is as 7555, it may be omitted in this Calculation, as making no considerable Alteration therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat air‑column weights as negligible relative to water unless extreme precision is required. The author explicitly states this simplification will not commit any mistake worth notice in many fountain calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic paradox: pressure at a base depends on depth, not total quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Water in each of these Tubes severally will press on the Base C with the same Weight; and that therefore ... all three of them operating together, will press with no more than the same Weight ... though taken together they contain much more water. 'This Pressure is perform'd not by a Fluid actually put in Motion, but by a quiescent one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by experiments with several tubes of different shapes/amounts: even if tubes contain different volumes, provided the vertical height to the communicating base is the same, the pressure on the base equals that due to that height alone. The text gives experiments and thought exercises to convince readers who might naturally think pressure sums with volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of pressure on equal parts of the same horizontal plane
rubrics_metrics.description: All the like Parts in the same Horizontal Plane are press'd alike; every equal Part ... of the said Horizontal Plane ... will be press'd downwards equally in all its Parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two points lie on the same horizontal fluid plane (connected by a fluid path not crossing other media), they experience equal pressure. The author uses this as a fundamental law to derive paradoxes and compute forces; the 'thread' (path) test is suggested to confirm connectedness of regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission of pressure in a fluid (small column produces large resultant on cover)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Whole square Cover ... will be rais'd up with the Force: of 326500 Pounds, including the Orifice VR, And that which presses on it. ... a small Quantity of Water in the Tube did not only lift up the Lid or Bottom ... but like wise bent the said Lid outwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative experiments (e.g., Mariotte) show a small column of fluid, when arranged with a large communicating reservoir and depth, can produce very large transmitted forces on covers or bottoms. Use these setups to demonstrate Pascal‑type transmission of pressure and the necessity of strong vessels to resist it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure in a fluid is proportional to depth (law of pressure according to the depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: These many thousand Parts of which Fluids consist, ... observe so accurately these Laws of Height ... the Law of Preſſure according to the Depth. ... the Pressure of the Air at LM within Chamber, is only as 1 to 2500 of that which happens at PQ by the Air out of the Chamber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply proportional reasoning using column heights (and comparative densities where required, e.g., mercury vs water vs air) to compute relative pressures. The barometer/mercury example is used to relate atmospheric column heights to equivalent water heights and to compute interior vs exterior pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curved tube behaviour: unequal heights and the role of air columns
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Motion of Water in a Curve Tube ... when the Finger is remov'd from V, the Water will subside from A to F, ... because the downward‑pressing Force upon F, or a added to b, is greater than the Force pressing upward express'd by a and c; consequently the Part F is press'd downwards by the Difference ... that is by b less c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing U‑ or curved tubes with trapped air, compare weights of water columns and the matched air columns; removing a temporary seal (finger) changes which air column acts and thus can reverse expected motion. Use symbolic letters for columns (a,b,c,d,e) and compute differences to predict motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental construction guidance for fountains and apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure is thus: ... two smaller, and every where Air‑tight Cisterns ... each of these has an Orifice or Hole ... and both of 'em may be render'd also Air tight, by stopping them with a Cork covered with a wet Bladder, or a Cock. ... On the Top of this last Tube, we fix another Plate, which was cover'd with a flat Plate, having a small round Hole in the Middle of it, through which the Stream was to pass, and we clos'd it at the Joint ... so that it was impervious either to Water or Air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical details: use air‑tight cisterns, corks covered with wet bladder, stop‑cocks, small plates with holes; invert and fill configurations as described; use fingers to temporarily plug small orifices when initiating experiments; stop‑cocks can replace awkward inversions or finger‑blocking in more convenient designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation method: subtract weights of opposing air/water columns
rubrics_metrics.description: This Difference is found by Substracting the smallest downward‑pressing Force a and e together ... from the greatest a, b and d together, less c ... So that the Difference, or the Force wherewith the Water ascends ... is equal to b and d, less e and less e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithmic rule: identify all upward‑pressing and downward‑pressing column contributions (label them), sum each group, then subtract the smaller (downward) from the larger (upward) to find net force. The text provides worked symbol algebra and numeric substitution to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small quantities arranged at great depth can produce enormous pressures at a base
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole Tube RQ does alone contain a cubical Foot, or 63 Pounds of Water ... the solid Contents of the Vessel ABTP ... 5184 cubical Feet ... the whole Mass of Water will weigh 326592 Pounds: With which Weight the loose Bottom WZ is burden'd and press'd by the little Water in the Tube ... far from raising the Bottom WZ by adding another Weight W (of 100 or 1000 Pounds either) ... there would be required a Weight of above 326000 Pounds, only to equiponderate, or rather to put in Motion the 63 Pounds of Water thus disposed in the Tube QR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates via equilibrium and scale thought‑experiment that a small mass of water in a tall connected column can demand enormous counterweight due to the arrangement and the large communicating reservoir. Use such experiments to emphasize the need for vessel strength and to illustrate paradoxical consequences of the depth–pressure law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical/physical implication: hydrostatic laws necessary to avoid catastrophic consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Without the Laws of Fluids, all Nature would be in. ... all the Chambers of Houses ... would be nothing else but fatal Caverns and a heap of Rubbish ... if the Air should exert its Gravitation ... like a Heap of small solid Bodies, and consequently that there were no other than a perpendicular Pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the law that pressure acts equally in a horizontal plane (and depends on depth) to reason about macroscopic stability (buildings, human habitability). The author provides a conceptual application relating barometer heights and comparative pressures as an argument for the physical necessity and explanatory power of hydrostatic laws.
